what_it_does: Serving a large AI language model in production means running it across many GPUs simultaneously, and in the real world those GPUs are not identical — a cluster may contain a mix of older and newer GPU models with different amounts of memory, different processing speeds, and network connections of different speeds between them. Existing systems either ignore this heterogeneity or handle compute and networking separately, leading to inefficient use of the available hardware. Helix treats the entire cluster as a mathematical flow network: each GPU is a node, and the directed edges between nodes carry a capacity that encodes both how fast that GPU computes and how fast the network link between those GPUs can transfer data. It then applies a classical algorithm — maximum flow, which finds the fastest possible movement of work through a network without exceeding any link's capacity — reformulated as a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) optimization, to simultaneously decide which layers of the model sit on which GPU and how incoming requests are routed through the cluster. By solving placement and routing together rather than independently, Helix can better exploit fast GPUs without creating network bottlenecks, and vice versa.
